Every test so far compared means across groups. Today both variables are continuous. **Correlation** asks whether two variables are linearly associated. **Regression** asks how much one changes per unit of the other, and predicts one from the other. Same recipe: H₀ as math, α first, look, check, test, conclude.

Lecture A012 used *Iris versicolor*. Here you use Adelie penguins: does flipper length go with body mass? Same workflow, so the logic transfers even though the numbers differ.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Correlation or regression? (click to expand)

|   | Correlation | Regression |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Question | Are X and Y linearly associated? | How much does Y change per unit X? |
| Symmetry | Swap X and Y, same *r* | Y is predicted from X; swapping changes the line |
| Output | One number, *r*, with a p-value and CI | A line: intercept and slope, each with a p-value |
| Prediction | None | Y for a new X |
| H₀ | true correlation = 0 | true slope = 0 |
| R | `cor()`, `cor.test()` | `lm()`, `summary()` |

Correlation is the right tool when neither variable is the cause, as with two exam scores. Regression is the right tool when one variable is the explanatory one, as with a dose you set and a response you measure.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Functions in this activity (click to expand)

| Function | What it does | Example |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| `cov(x, y)` | Covariance: do X and Y move together? Sign is meaningful, size depends on units | `cov(penguin_data$flipper_length_mm, penguin_data$body_mass_g)` |
| `cor(x, y)` | Pearson's *r*: covariance divided by both standard deviations, so it runs from −1 to 1 | `cor(x, y)` |
| `cor.test(x, y)` | *r* with a p-value and 95% CI; H₀ is true correlation = 0 | `cor.test(x, y)` |
| `lm(y ~ x, data = )` | Fits the least-squares line | `lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm, data = penguin_data)` |
| `summary(model)` | Intercept, slope, their p-values, and R² | `summary(lm_model)` |
| `coef(model)` | Just the intercept and slope | `coef(lm_model)` |
| `residuals(model)` | Observed minus predicted, one per row | `shapiro.test(residuals(lm_model))` |
| `plot(model, which = 1)` | Residuals vs fitted: linearity and equal spread |  |
| `plot(model, which = 4)` | Cook's distance per observation: which points move the fit |  |
| `cooks.distance(model)` | The numbers behind that plot | `max(cooks.distance(lm_model))` |
| `geom_smooth(method = "lm")` | Draws the fitted line and its 95% band on a scatterplot |  |

`cor.test()` returns the same kind of object as `t.test()`, so `$estimate`, `$p.value`, and `$conf.int` work. `summary(lm_model)$r.squared` pulls R² out of a model summary.
:::

Three clusters. Gentoo sit high and right, Adelie low and left, Chinstrap in between. A line through all 344 would mostly be measuring the gap between species, not flipper length. So, as in lecture, pick one species.

```{webr}
#| envir: regression_lab
#| exercise: scatter_all

had_error <- any(vapply(.evaluate_result, inherits, logical(1), "error"))
find_plot <- function(v, env) {
  if (inherits(v, "ggplot")) return(v)
  for (nm in rev(ls(env))) {
    o <- get(nm, envir = env)
    if (inherits(o, "ggplot")) return(o)
  }
  NULL
}
layer_class <- function(p, part) vapply(p$layers, function(l) class(l[[part]])[1], character(1))
plot_maps <- function(p) {
  m <- c(as.list(p$mapping), unlist(lapply(p$layers, function(l) as.list(l$mapping)), recursive = FALSE))
  names(m) <- sub(".*\\.", "", names(m))
  m
}
p <- find_plot(.last_value, .envir_result)
maps <- if (is.null(p)) list() else plot_maps(p)
col_var <- if (!is.null(maps$colour)) rlang::as_label(maps$colour) else NULL
if (had_error) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "R stopped. Read the last line of the message. Layers are joined with `+`.")
} else if (is.null(p)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "No figure yet. Keep the `ggplot()` call and add `geom_point()` with `+`.")
} else if (!"GeomPoint" %in% layer_class(p, "geom")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "A figure, but no points. Add `geom_point()`.")
} else if (!identical(col_var, "species")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Points drawn. Keep `color = species` inside `aes()` so the three species show as three colors.")
} else if (!exists("scatter_all", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Scatterplot drawn. Save it as `scatter_all` with `<-`.")
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
       message = "Three clusters, one per species. That is why the next step keeps only Adelie.")
}
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check yourself

1.  Which variable is X (explanatory) and which is Y (response) in "does flipper length predict body mass"?
2.  Would swapping them change *r*? Would it change the regression line?
3.  Why fit within one species instead of all 344 penguins?

**Answers:** flipper length is X, body mass is Y. Swapping leaves *r* unchanged but gives a different line, because regression minimizes vertical distances to Y. Pooling species would make the line measure the species gap rather than the within-species relationship, like the pooled sepal plot in lecture where *r* flipped from +0.53 to −0.12.
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: regression_lab
#| exercise: scatter_lm
#| check: true
had_error <- any(vapply(.evaluate_result, inherits, logical(1), "error"))
find_plot <- function(v, env) {
  if (inherits(v, "ggplot")) return(v)
  for (nm in rev(ls(env))) {
    o <- get(nm, envir = env)
    if (inherits(o, "ggplot")) return(o)
  }
  NULL
}
layer_class <- function(p, part) vapply(p$layers, function(l) class(l[[part]])[1], character(1))
smooth_method <- function(p) {
  for (l in p$layers) if (inherits(l$geom, "GeomSmooth")) {
    m <- l$stat_params$method
    return(if (is.null(m)) "auto" else as.character(m))
  }
  NULL
}
p <- find_plot(.last_value, .envir_result)
if (had_error) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "R stopped. Read the last line of the message. Layers are joined with `+`, and `method = \"lm\"` goes inside `geom_smooth()`.")
} else if (is.null(p)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "No figure yet. Keep the `ggplot()` call and add `geom_point()` with `+`.")
} else if (!"GeomPoint" %in% layer_class(p, "geom")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "A figure, but no points. Add `geom_point()`.")
} else if (!"GeomSmooth" %in% layer_class(p, "geom")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Points drawn. Add the fitted line with `geom_smooth(method = \"lm\")`.")
} else if (!identical(smooth_method(p), "lm")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
       message = "A smooth curve, not a straight line. Set `method = \"lm\"` inside `geom_smooth()`.")
} else if (!exists("scatter_lm", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Plot drawn. Save it as `scatter_lm` with `<-`.")
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
       message = "Points plus the least-squares line and its confidence band.")
}
```

## Part B: Correlation

**Research question:** Are flipper length and body mass linearly associated in Adelie penguins?

H₀: the true correlation is 0. Hₐ: it is not 0. Pearson correlation, α = 0.05.

### 5. Covariance depends on the ruler

Covariance measures whether X and Y move together: each penguin contributes (x − x̄)(y − ȳ), and the average of those products is the covariance. Compute it for flipper length and body mass and save it as `cov_raw`. Then compute it again with flipper length in **centimeters** (divide by 10) and body mass in **kilograms** (divide by 1000), and save that as `cov_rescaled`. Print both.

```{webr}
#| envir: regression_lab
#| setup: true
#| exercise: covariance
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
penguin_data <- penguins |>
  filter(species == "Adelie", !is.na(body_mass_g), !is.na(flipper_length_mm))
```

```{webr}
#| envir: regression_lab
#| exercise: covariance
cov_raw <-
cov_rescaled <-

```

:::: {.hint exercise="covariance"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

`cov()` takes two vectors. You can divide a column right inside the call.

``` r
cov(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
cov(mtcars$wt * 1000, mtcars$mpg)
```
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="covariance"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
cov_raw <- cov(penguin_data$flipper_length_mm, penguin_data$body_mass_g)
cov_rescaled <- cov(penguin_data$flipper_length_mm / 10, penguin_data$body_mass_g / 1000)
cov_raw
cov_rescaled
```

1404 mm·g versus 0.14 cm·kg. Same penguins, same picture, a number 10,000 times smaller. The sign is useful; the size depends on the units. That is why we need *r*.
:::
::::

```{webr}
#| envir: regression_lab
#| exercise: covariance
#| check: true
had_error <- any(vapply(.evaluate_result, inherits, logical(1), "error"))
if (had_error) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "R stopped. Read the last line of the message. `cov()` needs two vectors separated by a comma, each pulled out with `$`.")
} else if (!exists("cov_raw", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE) ||
           !exists("cov_rescaled", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Create both `cov_raw` and `cov_rescaled`.")
} else {
  a <- get("cov_raw", envir = .envir_result)
  b <- get("cov_rescaled", envir = .envir_result)
  ok <- function(v) is.numeric(v) && length(v) == 1 && !is.na(v)
  if (!ok(a) || !ok(b)) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
         message = "Both objects should be single numbers from `cov()`.")
  } else if (abs(a - 1404.03) > 1) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
         message = paste0("`cov_raw` = ", round(a, 2), ". Use flipper length and body mass from `penguin_data` in their original units."))
  } else if (abs(b - 0.1404) > 0.001) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
         message = paste0("`cov_rescaled` = ", signif(b, 4), ". Divide flipper length by 10 and body mass by 1000; the answer should be about 0.14."))
  } else {
    list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
         message = "1404 in mm and g, 0.14 in cm and kg. Same association, a number 10,000 times smaller.")
  }
}
```

### 6. From covariance to *r*

Dividing the covariance by both standard deviations removes the units: *r* = cov(x, y) / (sₓ · sᵧ). Compute it that way and save it as `r_by_hand`. Then compute it with `cor()` and save it as `r_cor`. Print both.

```{webr}
#| envir: regression_lab
#| setup: true
#| exercise: r_by_hand
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
penguin_data <- penguins |>
  filter(species == "Adelie", !is.na(body_mass_g), !is.na(flipper_length_mm))
cov_raw <- cov(penguin_data$flipper_length_mm, penguin_data$body_mass_g)
```

```{webr}
#| envir: regression_lab
#| exercise: r_by_hand
r_by_hand <-
r_cor <-

```

:::: {.hint exercise="r_by_hand"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

You already have `cov_raw`. Divide it by `sd()` of flipper length times `sd()` of body mass. `cor()` takes the same two vectors `cov()` did.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="r_by_hand"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
r_by_hand <- cov_raw / (sd(penguin_data$flipper_length_mm) * sd(penguin_data$body_mass_g))
r_cor <- cor(penguin_data$flipper_length_mm, penguin_data$body_mass_g)
r_by_hand
r_cor
```

Both are 0.468. Positive, moderate. Try the same division with `cov_rescaled` and the rescaled standard deviations: still 0.468. *r* does not care about the ruler.
:::
::::

```{webr}
#| envir: regression_lab
#| exercise: r_by_hand
#| check: true
had_error <- any(vapply(.evaluate_result, inherits, logical(1), "error"))
if (had_error) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "R stopped. Read the last line of the message. Put the product of the two `sd()` calls in parentheses before dividing.")
} else if (!exists("r_by_hand", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE) ||
           !exists("r_cor", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Create both `r_by_hand` and `r_cor`.")
} else {
  a <- get("r_by_hand", envir = .envir_result)
  b <- get("r_cor", envir = .envir_result)
  ok <- function(v) is.numeric(v) && length(v) == 1 && !is.na(v)
  if (!ok(a) || !ok(b)) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
         message = "Both objects should be single numbers.")
  } else if (abs(b - 0.4682) > 0.002) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
         message = paste0("`r_cor` = ", round(b, 3), ". Use `cor()` on flipper length and body mass in `penguin_data`."))
  } else if (abs(a - 0.4682) > 0.002) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
         message = paste0("`r_cor` is right, but `r_by_hand` = ", signif(a, 3), ". Divide `cov_raw` by `sd(x) * sd(y)`, with the product in parentheses."))
  } else {
    list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
         message = "r = 0.468 both ways. Covariance over the two standard deviations is the correlation.")
  }
}
```

### 7. *r* needs a p-value

*r* = 0.47 from 151 penguins is not the same evidence as *r* = 0.47 from 8. Run `cor.test()` on flipper length and body mass. Save it as `cor_result` and print it.

```{webr}
#| envir: regression_lab
#| setup: true
#| exercise: cor_result
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
penguin_data <- penguins |>
  filter(species == "Adelie", !is.na(body_mass_g), !is.na(flipper_length_mm))
```

*r* = 0.47, t = 6.47, df = 149, p = 1.3 × 10⁻⁹, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.58. The interval does not include 0.

```{webr}
#| envir: regression_lab
#| exercise: cor_result
#| check: true
had_error <- any(vapply(.evaluate_result, inherits, logical(1), "error"))
if (had_error) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "R stopped. Read the last line of the message. `cor.test()` takes two vectors separated by a comma.")
} else if (!exists("cor_result", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Save the result as `cor_result` with `<-`, then print it.")
} else {
  cr <- get("cor_result", envir = .envir_result)
  if (is.numeric(cr) && length(cr) == 1) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
         message = "That is `cor()`, a single number. `cor.test()` adds the p-value and confidence interval.")
  } else if (!inherits(cr, "htest") || is.null(cr$estimate)) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
         message = "`cor_result` should be the output of `cor.test()`.")
  } else if (abs(unname(cr$estimate) - 0.4682) < 0.002) {
    list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
         message = "r = 0.47, p = 1.3e-9, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.58. The interval excludes zero.")
  } else {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
         message = paste0("A correlation test, but r = ", round(unname(cr$estimate), 3), ". Use flipper length and body mass from `penguin_data`."))
  }
}
```

```{webr}

#| exercise: assoc_call

if (had_error) {

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check yourself

Three studies all report *r* = 0.30. One has n = 8, one n = 30, one n = 300. Which is the strongest evidence that the true correlation is not zero?

**Answer:** n = 300 (p ≈ 10⁻⁷). With n = 8 the same *r* gives p = 0.47; with n = 30, p = 0.11. *r* measures strength in the sample; p measures how surprising that *r* would be if the true value were 0, and that depends on n.
:::

## Part C: Linear regression

**Research question:** How much heavier is an Adelie penguin per extra millimeter of flipper?

H₀: the true slope is 0. Hₐ: it is not 0. Least-squares regression of body mass on flipper length, α = 0.05.

library(tidyverse)

penguin_data <- penguins |>

Same formula shape as `aov()`: response, tilde, explanatory variable, `data =`. Response goes on the left.

summary(fit)
```
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="lm_model"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
lm_model <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm, data = penguin_data)
summary(lm_model)
```

Slope 32.8 g per mm, p = 1.3 × 10⁻⁹. Intercept −2536 g. Multiple R-squared 0.219. The slope's p-value is the same as `cor.test()` gave: with one predictor they are the same test.
:::
::::

```{webr}
#| envir: regression_lab
#| exercise: lm_model
#| check: true
had_error <- any(vapply(.evaluate_result, inherits, logical(1), "error"))
if (had_error) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "R stopped. Read the last line of the message. The formula is `body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm`, and the table goes in `data = penguin_data`.")
} else if (!exists("lm_model", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Save the model as `lm_model` with `<-`, then print `summary(lm_model)`.")
} else {
  m <- get("lm_model", envir = .envir_result)
  if (!inherits(m, "lm") || inherits(m, "aov")) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
         message = "`lm_model` should come from `lm()`.")
  } else {
    b <- unname(coef(m))
    if (length(b) == 2 && abs(b[2] - 32.83) < 0.5) {
      list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
           message = "Slope 32.8 g per mm, p = 1.3e-9, R-squared 0.219.")
    } else if (length(b) == 2 && abs(b[2] - 0.00668) < 0.0005) {
      list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
           message = "The formula is backwards: this predicts flipper length from body mass. Put `body_mass_g` on the left of the `~`.")
    } else {
      list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
           message = paste0("A linear model, but the slope is ", signif(b[2], 3), ". Fit `body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm` with `data = penguin_data`."))
    }
  }
}
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check yourself

1.  The slope is 32.8. What does it mean?
2.  The intercept is −2536 g. What should you make of it?

**Answers:** (1) Each extra millimeter of flipper goes with about 33 g more body mass, on average. Not "mass equals 33 times flipper length", and not "flipper length explains 33% of mass". (2) It is the predicted mass of a penguin with a 0 mm flipper. Flippers in this sample run from 172 to 210 mm, so X = 0 is far outside the data and the intercept has no biological meaning. It is just where the line crosses the axis. The model is still fine.
:::

### 10. R² by hand

R² is the fraction of the scatter in Y that the line accounts for. Compute the sum of squared distances from each body mass to the **mean** body mass and save it as `ss_mean`. Compute the sum of squared **residuals** and save it as `ss_line`. Then compute `r_squared_by_hand` as 1 − `ss_line` / `ss_mean`. Print all three.

```{webr}
#| envir: regression_lab
#| setup: true
#| exercise: r_squared_by_hand
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
penguin_data <- penguins |>
  filter(species == "Adelie", !is.na(body_mass_g), !is.na(flipper_length_mm))
lm_model <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm, data = penguin_data)
```

```{webr}
#| envir: regression_lab
#| exercise: r_squared_by_hand
ss_mean <-
ss_line <-
r_squared_by_hand <-

```

:::: {.hint exercise="r_squared_by_hand"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

A sum of squares is `sum((values)^2)`. For `ss_mean` the values are `body_mass_g - mean(body_mass_g)`. For `ss_line` they are `residuals(lm_model)`, which are already observed minus predicted.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="r_squared_by_hand"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
ss_mean <- sum((penguin_data$body_mass_g - mean(penguin_data$body_mass_g))^2)
ss_line <- sum(residuals(lm_model)^2)
r_squared_by_hand <- 1 - ss_line / ss_mean
ss_mean
ss_line
r_squared_by_hand
```

Scatter around the mean is 31.5 million g²; around the line it is 24.6 million. The line removed 22% of the scatter, so R² = 0.219. And 0.468² = 0.219: with one predictor, R² is *r* squared.
:::
::::

```{webr}
#| envir: regression_lab
#| exercise: r_squared_by_hand
#| check: true
had_error <- any(vapply(.evaluate_result, inherits, logical(1), "error"))
need <- c("ss_mean", "ss_line", "r_squared_by_hand")
if (had_error) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "R stopped. Read the last line of the message. Square the vector inside `sum()`: `sum((...)^2)`.")
} else if (!all(vapply(need, exists, logical(1), envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Create all three: `ss_mean`, `ss_line`, and `r_squared_by_hand`.")
} else {
  sm <- get("ss_mean", envir = .envir_result)
  sl <- get("ss_line", envir = .envir_result)
  r2 <- get("r_squared_by_hand", envir = .envir_result)
  ok <- function(v) is.numeric(v) && length(v) == 1 && !is.na(v)
  if (!ok(sm) || !ok(sl) || !ok(r2)) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
         message = "All three objects should be single numbers.")
  } else if (abs(sm - 31542434) > 1000) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
         message = paste0("`ss_mean` = ", signif(sm, 4), ". It should be `sum((body_mass_g - mean(body_mass_g))^2)`, about 31.5 million."))
  } else if (abs(sl - 24627928) > 1000) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
         message = paste0("`ss_line` = ", signif(sl, 4), ". It should be `sum(residuals(lm_model)^2)`, about 24.6 million."))
  } else if (abs(r2 - 0.2192) > 0.001) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
         message = "Both sums of squares are right. `r_squared_by_hand` should be `1 - ss_line / ss_mean`.")
  } else {
    list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
         message = "R-squared = 0.219 by hand: the line removes 22% of the scatter around the mean.")
  }
}
```

### 12. Residuals vs fitted

Regression makes four assumptions: a linear relationship, independent observations, normal residuals, and equal spread of residuals along the line. Independence comes from the design (each penguin measured once). The other three are checked on the residuals, after the fit. Run the block: `plot(lm_model, which = 1)` draws each residual against its fitted value.

```{webr}

  filter(species == "Adelie", !is.na(body_mass_g), !is.na(flipper_length_mm))
lm_model <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm, data = penguin_data)
```

```{webr}
#| envir: regression_lab

```

You are looking for two things: no curve (linearity) and no fan (equal spread). A shapeless cloud around the dashed zero line is what you want.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="plot_residuals"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

A shapeless cloud. The red trend line wobbles but does not curve, and the spread is about the same at small and large fitted values. Linearity and equal spread look fine. R labels the three largest residuals by row number; that is information, not an instruction to delete them.
:::
::::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check yourself

Study 1: R² = 0.02, p \< 0.001, n = 3000. Study 2: R² = 0.85, p = 0.08, n = 5. Which statement is best?

A.  Study 1 found the stronger relationship\
B.  Study 2 found the stronger relationship\
C.  Study 2 found a significant relationship\
D.  Neither study found a relationship

**Answer:** B. R² is strength; p is evidence. Study 2's relationship is far stronger, but five points are not enough to rule out chance. Study 1's is certain to exist and almost too small to matter. Report both numbers, always.
:::

## Part D: One point can rotate the line

A regression line is pulled toward every point, but not equally. A point far out along X has extra leverage: it can rotate the whole line. The Adelie data has no such point, so this part uses a small made-up dataset of 31 points, the same demonstration as in lecture A012. You will see the point, measure how much it moves the slope, and decide what to do about it.

ggplot(lev_plus, aes(x = x, y = y)) +

## Solution

``` r
lm_lev <- lm(y ~ x, data = lev_plus)
lev_without <- lev_plus |>
  filter(x < 20)
lm_without <- lm(y ~ x, data = lev_without)
slope_with <- coef(lm_lev)[2]
slope_without <- coef(lm_without)[2]
slope_with
slope_without
```

Slope 0.40 with the point, 0.92 without it. One observation out of 31 cut the slope by more than half. To see both lines on the same plot, add a second `geom_smooth()` that uses only the 30 ordinary points:

``` r
ggplot(lev_plus, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(data = lev_without, method = "lm", se = FALSE)
```
:::
::::

```{webr}
#| envir: regression_lab
#| exercise: fit_twice
#| check: true
had_error <- any(vapply(.evaluate_result, inherits, logical(1), "error"))
need <- c("lm_lev", "lev_without", "lm_without", "slope_with", "slope_without")
have <- vapply(need, exists, logical(1), envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)
if (had_error) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "R stopped. Read the last line of the message. The model is `lm(y ~ x, data = ...)`, and the filter condition is `x < 20`.")
} else if (!all(have)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = paste0("Still missing: `", paste(need[!have], collapse = "`, `"), "`."))
} else {
  m1 <- get("lm_lev", envir = .envir_result)
  lw <- get("lev_without", envir = .envir_result)
  m2 <- get("lm_without", envir = .envir_result)
  sw <- get("slope_with", envir = .envir_result)
  so <- get("slope_without", envir = .envir_result)
  ok <- function(v) is.numeric(v) && length(v) == 1 && !is.na(v)
  if (!inherits(m1, "lm") || !inherits(m2, "lm")) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
         message = "`lm_lev` and `lm_without` should both come from `lm()`.")
  } else if (!is.data.frame(lw) || nrow(lw) != 30) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
         message = paste0("`lev_without` has ", if (is.data.frame(lw)) nrow(lw) else "?", " rows. Keep the 30 points with `x < 20`."))
  } else if (abs(unname(coef(m1))[2] - 0.404) > 0.01) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
         message = paste0("`lm_lev` has slope ", signif(unname(coef(m1))[2], 3), ". Fit `y ~ x` on all of `lev_plus`."))
  } else if (abs(unname(coef(m2))[2] - 0.916) > 0.01) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
         message = paste0("`lm_without` has slope ", signif(unname(coef(m2))[2], 3), ". Fit `y ~ x` on `lev_without`."))
  } else if (!ok(sw) || !ok(so)) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
         message = "`slope_with` and `slope_without` should each be one number: `coef(model)[2]`.")
  } else if (abs(unname(sw) - 0.404) > 0.01 || abs(unname(so) - 0.916) > 0.01) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
         message = "Both models are right, but the saved slopes do not match them. `coef(model)[1]` is the intercept; the slope is `[2]`.")
  } else {
    list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
         message = "Slope 0.40 with the point, 0.92 without it. One observation more than halved the slope.")
  }
}
```

### 17. Cook's distance

Cook's distance puts a number on what you just saw: for each observation, how much the fitted line would move if that observation were removed. Run `plot(lm_lev, which = 4)`. Then compute the rule-of-thumb cutoff `cook_cut` as 4 divided by the number of rows, and `max_cook` as the largest value of `cooks.distance(lm_lev)`. Print both.

        7.13, 11.07, 4.78, 8.61, 1.18, 1.47, 3.51, 7.96, 3.53, 10.44,
        9.89, 4.94, 5.62, 9.68, 7.81, 4.12, 9.39, 4.74, 4.71, 5.04, 4))

:::: {.hint exercise="cooks"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

`nrow(lev_plus)` is the number of observations. `cooks.distance()` returns one number per row; `max()` picks the largest.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="cooks"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
plot(lm_lev, which = 4)
cook_cut <- 4 / nrow(lev_plus)
max_cook <- max(cooks.distance(lm_lev))
cook_cut
max_cook
```

One bar per observation; R labels the three largest. Observation 31 has Cook's distance 11, about 85 times the 4/n cutoff of 0.13. Every other bar is below the cutoff. One point is doing all the work, and this plot finds it even when the scatterplot is too crowded to see it.
:::
::::

```{webr}
#| envir: regression_lab
#| exercise: cooks
#| check: true
had_error <- any(vapply(.evaluate_result, inherits, logical(1), "error"))
if (had_error) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "R stopped. Read the last line of the message. `cooks.distance()` takes the model `lm_lev`; `nrow()` takes the table `lev_plus`.")
} else if (!exists("cook_cut", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE) ||
           !exists("max_cook", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Create both `cook_cut` and `max_cook`.")
} else {
  cc <- get("cook_cut", envir = .envir_result)
  mc <- get("max_cook", envir = .envir_result)
  ok <- function(v) is.numeric(v) && length(v) == 1 && !is.na(v)
  if (!ok(cc) || !ok(mc)) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
         message = "Both objects should be single numbers.")
  } else if (abs(cc - 4 / 31) > 0.002) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
         message = paste0("`cook_cut` = ", signif(cc, 3), ". It should be `4 / nrow(lev_plus)`, which is 4 / 31."))
  } else if (abs(mc - 11.0) > 0.2) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
         message = paste0("`max_cook` = ", signif(mc, 3), ". Use `max(cooks.distance(lm_lev))`; it should be about 11."))
  } else {
    list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
         message = "Cutoff 0.13, largest Cook's distance 11. Observation 31 moves the fit; nothing else comes close.")
  }
}
```

:::

## 19. Recap: functions you practiced

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What does each function do?

| Function | Role |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `ggplot()` + `geom_point()` with `color = species` | Plot first; look for groups |
| `filter()` | One species, no missing values |
| `geom_smooth(method = "lm")` | Fitted line and its confidence band |
| `cov(x, y)` | Direction of association; size depends on units |
| `cor(x, y)` | *r*: covariance over both standard deviations, −1 to 1 |
| `cor.test(x, y)` | *r* with p-value and CI; H₀: true correlation = 0 |
| `lm(y ~ x, data = )` | Least-squares line |
| `summary(lm_model)` | Intercept, slope, p-values, R² |
| `sum((y - mean(y))^2)` and `sum(residuals(model)^2)` | SS around the mean and around the line |
| `summary(lm_model)$r.squared` | R² = 1 − SS_line / SS_mean = *r*² |
| `plot(model, which = 1)` | Residuals vs fitted: linearity and equal spread |
| `shapiro.test(residuals(model))` | Normality of residuals |
| `coef(model)[2]` | The slope, to compare fits with and without a point |
| `plot(model, which = 4)` and `cooks.distance(model)` | Which observation moves the fit |
| `4 / nrow(data)` | Rule-of-thumb Cook's distance cutoff |

If you can explain each row in your own words, you have covered **Coding Assignment 4, Part D** and lecture A012.
:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Three things to say in your write-up

1.  **Slope, p, and R² are three different facts.** "33 g per mm (p = 1.3 × 10⁻⁹, R² = 0.22)" says how much, how sure, and how much is explained. A tiny p with a tiny R² is a real but weak relationship. A big R² with p = 0.08 is a strong pattern you cannot yet trust.
2.  **Association is not cause.** Nothing was manipulated. Longer flippers go with heavier bodies; neither causes the other.
3.  **Report influence honestly.** If one point moves the slope, give the fit with it and without it, say where the gap in X is, and let the reader see that the conclusion rests on one observation. Do not delete it to make the line behave.
:::

## Keep playing

**What pooling would have done.** Fit the penguin regression on all three species together.

```{webr}
#| envir: regression_lab
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
all_penguins <- penguins |> filter(!is.na(body_mass_g), !is.na(flipper_length_mm))
summary(lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm, data = all_penguins))$r.squared
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
R² = 0.76 pooled, 0.22 within Adelie. Most of the pooled "prediction" is the species gap you saw in step 2. The lecture's iris sepal slide showed the same thing: pool the species and the relationship changes.
:::

**Pooling can flip the sign.** Within Adelie, bill length and bill depth are positively correlated. Across all three species, the correlation is negative.

```{webr}
#| envir: regression_lab
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
adelie <- penguins |> filter(species == "Adelie")
cor(adelie$bill_length_mm, adelie$bill_depth_mm, use = "complete.obs")
cor(penguins$bill_length_mm, penguins$bill_depth_mm, use = "complete.obs")
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
*r* = +0.39 within Adelie, −0.24 pooled. Gentoo have long, shallow bills, which drags the pooled line the other way. Plot first, look for groups.
:::

**Which analysis?** Match each design to a test.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check yourself

1.  Exam 1 and exam 2 scores for every student: are the two related?
2.  1000 adults: does blood pressure predict blood glucose?
3.  30 mice assigned to five caffeine doses; heart rate measured.
4.  60 bacterial colonies: diameter measured, each scored resistant or not. Does resistance relate to size?

**Answers:** (1) correlation; neither exam explains the other. (2) regression; one variable is named as the predictor. (3) regression; dose was set by the experimenter, so it is the explanatory variable, and the five doses are numbers on a scale, not just labels. (4) Welch *t*-test; one continuous variable (diameter) compared between two groups (resistant or not).
:::
